title: The light that entered Krishna
hook: a light rises from the fallen king and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira finishes his rite
carry: what the mind dwells on, it reaches

segments.voice: Yesterday Shishupala's hundred pardons ran out, and Krishna spoke to the kings before he acted. Kshama has a limit: dharma must be protected.

Shishupala has fallen, and the hall is silent. But the poem isn't done with him. Something rises from his body: a radiance, the text says, bright as the sun. Every eye in the hall follows it. It moves toward Krishna, bows to him, and enters him. The man who railed against Krishna in front of every king ends inside him. It's a strange ending, and the poem says the kings who saw it were amazed.
screen: `A LIGHT RISES FROM HIS BODY.` → `IT BOWS TO KRISHNA.` → `IT ENTERS HIM.`

segments.voice: What does it mean that Shishupala's light enters Krishna? The Mahabharata shows it and moves on. But Hindus asked the question, and a later scripture, the Bhagavata Purana, has Yudhishthira ask it out loud. The sage Narada answers: some came to Krishna through love, some through fear, and Shishupala through hatred, because all of them fixed their minds on him. He thought about Krishna constantly, and that single-minded attention carried him to Krishna in the end. The Gita puts it as a rule: whatever the mind dwells on at the last, that is where a person goes. So the teaching is about attention: the mind becomes what it holds. That's why so many Hindus practice remembering God on purpose, a name repeated, a picture kept close, so the mind's resting place is what they love. Other readers take the light more simply: everything that lives returns, at last, to its source. Then the story turns practical. Yudhishthira has the funeral rites performed for Shishupala and places Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi. The rite is finished, the guests are sent home, and Krishna returns to his own city. Look back at the week: seva at the Rajasuya, the first honor, gentle speech, held anger, a hundred pardons, the limit, and now the light. Shishupala's story ends here. But remember the cousin at the gift table. He's still in Indraprastha, and the next story is his.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE LIGHT MEAN?` · `NARADA: HE FIXED HIS MIND ON KRISHNA.` · `THE MIND BECOMES WHAT IT HOLDS.` · `THE RITE IS FINISHED.` · then, large: `WHAT THE MIND DWELLS ON, IT REACHES.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've had real trouble with, someone who takes up a lot of room in your thoughts. You don't have to change how you feel; just see your attention as a light you've been shining at them. With each slow breath, gather a little of it back, and set it on something you love. If you pray, rest it on a name of God, said quietly; if not, rest it on someone who makes you glad.
Shishupala. Krishna's cousin and fierce opponent, pardoned a hundred times, whose light rose at the end and entered Krishna.
Your line: what the mind dwells on, it reaches. Even Shishupala's hatred carried him to Krishna. Tomorrow, a hall that plays tricks. That's the week.

howItsDone: In the Bhagavata Purana (Book 7, chapter 1), Narada tells Yudhishthira that Shishupala reached Krishna by fixing his mind on him in enmity, and the Bhagavad Gita (8.6) says a person goes to whatever the mind dwells on at the end. The Mahabharata itself does not explain the light, and readers take it in more than one way.
